sections.history: Sirkazhi lies in the Kaveri delta between Chidambaram and Mayiladuthurai, and is one of the great Shaiva towns of Chola Nadu. The Tevaram hymns praise it as Sirkazhi and also as Brahmapuram, one of a dozen ancient names the town is said to have borne, which makes the temple a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Above all it is the birthplace of Tirugnana Sambandar, the child-saint whose hymns open the Tevaram, and the town has honoured his memory for well over a thousand years. The temple as it stands is a structure of the medieval Tamil country, enlarged by later patrons and kept in unbroken worship.
sections.architecture: The temple is unusual for rising in three levels, with a different form of Shiva in each. Brahmapureeswarar, the linga, is worshipped at ground level. Climbing a stair, the devotee reaches the shrine of Thoniappar, where Shiva sits with the goddess Periya Nayaki as though upon a boat, and a further stair leads to Sattainathar, the Bhairava form of the Lord, on the upper level. Sources differ on which level holds which shrine; the order given here is the one most widely recorded. On the outer prakara stands the shrine of Sambandar, with the shrine of Thirunilai Nayaki near it, and the great temple tank, the Brahma Theertham, lies at the heart of the complex, one of some twenty-two sacred waters tradition links with the place.
sections.legends: The place is named Brahmapuram because the god Brahma is said to have worshipped Shiva here. Another tradition tells that when a great deluge covered the world, Shiva and Uma floated on a boat, a thoni, and found Sirkazhi untouched by the waters; the Lord stayed on as Thoniappar. On the topmost level he is Sattainathar, the Bhairava who guards the town and is sought by those in troubles of the law. But the story that fills the temple with feeling is Sambandar's. As a small child he was left at the edge of the tank while his father, Sivapada Hridayar, went down to bathe, and he cried out for his parents. Shiva and Parvati appeared, and the Goddess fed him milk from a golden cup. When his father returned and saw the milk on the child's lips, the boy pointed toward the temple and sang his first hymn, the one beginning Todudaiya Seviyan.
sections.festivals: The Chithirai Thiruvadhirai festival in April and May is the temple's greatest celebration, and on its second day the feeding of Sambandar by the Goddess is enacted as the milk festival. After it, Sambandar is carried in procession to the neighbouring temple of Tirukolakka, where he is remembered receiving his golden cymbals. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed with devotion, and the Bhairava shrine draws special crowds on Ashtami days. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: A visit to Sirkazhi is a climb as much as a darshan. Begin at ground level with Brahmapureeswarar and the goddess, then take the stairs to Thoniappar and, at the top, to Sattainathar, feeling the temple lift above the town at each step. Many pilgrims go to the Sambandar shrine and to the tank where the child is said to have been fed, and parents often bring their children to receive a blessing for learning and speech. The temple stands in the heart of a busy market town, yet the upper shrines are quiet, and a morning visit is the most peaceful.

visit.timings: Commonly reported as roughly early morning to around midday and again from late afternoon to about nine in the evening; published timings vary between sources, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is usually allowed in the outer corridors and courtyards but not within the sanctums, as at temples across Tamil Nadu. Ask the temple staff before photographing rituals, priests or the upper shrines.
visit.gettingThere: Sirkazhi lies on the Chennai–Chidambaram–Mayiladuthurai road, about 17 km from Chidambaram and 58 km from Kumbakonam, and roughly 260 km from Chennai by road. The town has its own railway station on the Chennai–Mayiladuthurai line, and frequent buses serve it from the surrounding towns. The temple stands in the centre of the town, within easy reach of the bus stand and the station.
